intro: A raw egg drops from a stairwell and survives. A roller coaster train climbs one hill under a chain, then flies through a whole ride with no motor at all. A balloon rubbed on a sweater bends a stream of water without touching it. A steel railing and a wooden bench sit at the same temperature, yet one feels bitterly cold. Each of these is a puzzle you can picture, and each one has an answer you can test.

This unit is about forces and energy: the pushes and pulls that change how things move, and the energy that moves from place to place and form to form while the total never changes. You will meet Newton's three laws and use them to predict what a net force will do. You will see why a soft, slow stop protects an egg, a bike rider or a passenger in a crash. You will follow gravity from a falling pencil to the Moon's orbit, and follow heat through a spoon, a boiling pot and the empty space between the Sun and Earth.

By the end, you should be able to explain why a heavier cart is harder to speed up, why each roller coaster hill must be lower than the last, why a lid keeps cocoa hot, and where every Calorie in your lunch came from. You will also plan fair tests, read data tables, and weigh the trade-offs of the fuels that power Illinois. Forces and energy are the tools engineers use to build a safer car and a better cooler, and they are the tools you will use to explain the world you already see.
bigQuestion: How do forces change motion, and how does energy move and change form without ever disappearing?

timeline.t: Galileo publishes his ramp and pendulum experiments, arguing that all objects fall with the same acceleration
Isaac Newton's Principia lays out three laws of motion and one law of gravity for apples and planets alike
Count Rumford drills cannon barrels and argues that heat is motion, not a fluid, because it never runs out
William Herschel finds invisible infrared rays beyond the red end of the spectrum that warm a thermometer
Hans Christian Oersted sees a compass needle swing beside a wire carrying current: electricity makes magnetism
Michael Faraday shows that a moving magnet makes an electric current, the idea behind every generator
James Joule measures how much heat a falling weight makes as it turns a paddle wheel in water
The three-point seat belt is introduced in cars, spreading the stopping force across hips and chest
An Apollo 15 astronaut drops a hammer and a feather on the Moon; with no air, they land together
Great America opens in Gurnee, Illinois, and its coasters become a physics lesson for Chicago-area students

test.q: A sled is pushed with 15 newtons forward while friction pushes 5 newtons backward. What is the net force?
test.why: Opposite forces subtract: 15 minus 5 leaves 10 newtons in the forward direction.

test.q: A hockey puck slides across ice and keeps going for a long way. Which law explains this?
choices: Newton's first law: no net force, no change in motion
test.why: With very little friction on ice, there is almost no net force, so the puck keeps its speed and direction.

test.q: The same net force acts on a 1-kilogram ball and a 3-kilogram ball. Which is true?
choices: The 1-kilogram ball accelerates three times as much
test.why: Acceleration equals force divided by mass. Less mass with the same force means more acceleration.

test.q: A rocket pushes hot gas downward and rises. What force lifts the rocket?
choices: The air pushing on the nose
The gas pushing upward on the rocket
test.why: Forces come in pairs. The rocket pushes gas down, so the gas pushes the rocket up with an equal force.

test.q: Why does bending your knees when you land from a jump reduce the force on your legs?
choices: It makes the stop take longer, so the force is smaller
test.why: A longer stopping time means a smaller acceleration, and a smaller acceleration needs a smaller force.

test.q: A student tests whether foam padding protects an egg. Which is the variable?
test.why: The variable is the one thing changed on purpose. Everything else is kept the same as a control.

test.q: A 20-kilogram dog is taken to the Moon. What happens to its mass and weight?
choices: Mass stays 20 kilograms; weight drops to about one sixth
Mass drops; weight stays the same
test.why: Mass is the amount of matter and never changes. Weight is gravity's pull, and the Moon pulls about one sixth as hard.

test.q: Gravity between two objects gets weaker when what happens?
test.why: Gravity depends on mass and distance. More distance means a much weaker pull; more mass means a stronger one.

test.q: Two balloons rubbed on the same sweater push each other apart. Why?
choices: They carry the same kind of charge, and like charges repel
test.why: Rubbing gives both balloons the same charge, and like charges push apart.

test.q: An electromagnet stops working when the switch is turned off. What does this show?
choices: The magnetic field came from the electric current
test.why: Moving charge makes the magnetic field, as Oersted found. No current, no field.

test.q: A car doubles its speed. What happens to its kinetic energy and its stopping distance?
choices: Kinetic energy doubles; stopping distance stays the same
Both become about four times bigger
Kinetic energy becomes four times bigger; stopping distance is unchanged
test.why: Kinetic energy depends on speed squared, so it quadruples, and the brakes need about four times the distance to remove it.

test.q: A roller coaster's second hill is lower than its first. What explains this?
choices: Energy is conserved and some is lost to friction as heat, so the train cannot climb as high
The chain motor runs out of fuel
Gravity is weaker on the second hill
The train gains mass on the way down
test.why: The train's total energy was set at the top of the first hill, and friction and air drain some of it into heat on the way.

test.q: A cup of hot tea is left on a table. What happens to the heat?
choices: It stays in the cup forever
It flows from the cooler room into the tea
It flows from the tea into the cooler room by conduction, convection and radiation
test.why: Heat flows from warmer to cooler. It leaves through the cup walls, rising air and infrared radiation until the tea matches the room.

test.q: Which container would keep ice frozen the longest on a hot day?
choices: A thin metal bowl with no lid
A foam cooler with a tight lid
A glass jar with no lid
test.why: Foam full of trapped air slows conduction, and the lid stops warm air from carrying heat in by convection.

test.q: Where did the energy that powers your muscles come from?
choices: From the temperature of your body
From the air you breathe alone
From chemical energy stored in the bonds of the food you ate
test.why: Food stores chemical potential energy. Your body breaks it down with oxygen and releases the energy for motion, growth and heat.

write.prompt: Make a claim: which is the more important design idea for keeping an egg safe in a two-story drop, slowing the fall or stretching out the stop? Support your claim with evidence from the egg drop, the helmet and crumple zone lessons, and the fair test data, and explain the reasoning using Newton's laws and energy.

Give the other side a fair hearing: why might someone choose the other idea, and what evidence would change your mind?

title: Forces, Motion and Energy

chapters.title: Forces and Newton's Laws
chapters.bigQuestion: Why do things speed up, slow down, turn or stay still, and how can we predict it?

story.title: The Egg Drop
story.kicker: One raw egg, two stories of stairwell, and a design that has to stop it gently.
paragraphs: Maya stands at the top of the school stairwell with a raw egg. It sits inside a shell she built from a paper cup, three straws and a plastic grocery bag tied at the corners like a parachute. Below her, on the tile floor, the class has taped a target. The rule is simple: drop it from the second-floor railing, and the egg must survive.

The first team goes before her. Their egg is wrapped in tape and nothing else. It falls fast, hits with a sharp crack, and yellow yolk spreads across the tile. The floor stopped that egg in a tiny fraction of a second. All of its motion had to vanish almost at once, and the shell could not take that.

Maya lets go. The bag opens, catches the air, and the whole package drifts down slower than the first egg. When it lands, the straws bend and the cup crumples. The egg inside rolls out without a crack. The class cheers, but her teacher asks the harder question: why did it work?

Maya thinks it through. The parachute pushed against the air, so the egg never got going very fast. The straws and the crumpling cup made the stop take longer, a soft squish instead of a sharp crack. A gentler stop over more time means a smaller force on the egg. That is the same idea inside a bike helmet, a car bumper and the airbag in a steering wheel.

Every force in this chapter shows up in that stairwell. Gravity pulled the egg down. Air pushed up on the bag. The floor pushed up on the cup. Each push and pull changed how the egg moved, and each one can be measured and predicted. Isaac Newton wrote down the rules in 1687, and engineers still use them to design every car, bridge and spacecraft.
story.think: The taped egg and Maya's egg both fell the same distance. What was different about how each one stopped, and why did that matter?

lessons.title: Pushes, Pulls and Net Force
lessons.mainIdea: A force is a push or a pull with a size and a direction, and only the total, or net, force changes how something moves.
reading: Push a shopping cart and it rolls. Pull a wagon and it follows you. A *force* is any push or pull on an object. Every force has a size, measured in a unit called the *newton*, and a direction. One newton is about the weight of a small apple in your hand. A gentle push might be 5 newtons. A car engine can push with thousands.

Most objects have several forces on them at the same time. A book on a desk has gravity pulling it down and the desk pushing it up. Two students can push the same box from opposite sides. To predict what happens, you add the forces up, keeping track of direction. The total is called the *net force*.

If two forces are the same size and point in opposite directions, they cancel. The net force is zero, and the motion does not change. If one is bigger, the net force points in the direction of the bigger force. In a tug of war, the rope moves toward the team with the greater pull, and the difference between the two pulls is what moves it.

Drawing forces as arrows helps. A longer arrow means a bigger force, and the arrow points in the force's direction. Engineers draw these arrow diagrams for bridges, chairs and rockets before they build anything. The question is always the same: what is the net force, and which way does it point?

words.d: a push or a pull on an object; it has a size and a direction
the unit used to measure force; about the weight of a small apple
the total of all the forces on an object after opposite directions cancel

look.title: Two Pushes on One Box
look.text: A box sits on a smooth gym floor. Ana pushes it to the right with 30 newtons. Ben pushes it to the left with 20 newtons. The box starts sliding slowly to the right. Then a third student, Cal, joins Ben and adds 10 newtons of push to the left. The box slows and stops moving in either direction, even though three people are still pushing hard.
look.prompt: What is the net force on the box after Cal joins, and why does the box stop changing its motion even though everyone is still pushing?

check.q: Two students push a box from opposite sides with exactly 40 newtons each. What is the net force on the box?
check.why: Equal forces in opposite directions cancel, so the total is zero and the box's motion does not change.

check.q: Which of these best describes a force?
choices: A push or a pull with a size and a direction
Any kind of energy stored in an object
The speed at which something moves
The weight of an object only
check.why: A force is a push or a pull. Weight is one kind of force, but pushes from hands, engines and floors are forces too.

check.q: A rope in a tug of war moves to the left. What must be true?
choices: The left team pulled harder than the right team
Both teams pulled with equal force
check.why: The rope moves in the direction of the net force, which points toward the team pulling harder.

lessons.title: Motion Keeps Going
lessons.mainIdea: Newton's first law: with no net force, a resting object stays at rest and a moving object keeps moving at the same speed in a straight line.
reading: Slide a hockey puck across a rough rug and it stops fast. Slide it on ice and it glides far. On a perfectly smooth surface with no air, it would keep going forever. Nothing has to push it to keep it moving. This surprised people for a long time. Aristotle taught that objects needed a steady push to keep moving, and it took Galileo's ramp experiments and Newton's thinking to change that idea.

Newton's first law says an object's motion does not change unless a net force acts on it. A resting object stays put. A moving object keeps the same speed and the same direction. The tendency of objects to keep doing what they are doing is called *inertia*. The more mass an object has, the more inertia it has and the harder it is to change its motion.

You feel inertia every day. When a bus starts moving, your body wants to stay still, so you lurch backward. When the bus brakes, your body wants to keep moving, so you pitch forward. A seat belt gives the force that stops you with the car. Without it, you keep moving until the dashboard or the windshield stops you instead.

So why do things on Earth slow down? Because forces like *friction* and air resistance are always acting. Friction is a force between surfaces that rub, and it always pushes against motion. The puck on the rug did not stop by itself; friction stopped it. Remove the friction, and the first law shows itself clearly, as it does for a probe coasting through deep space.

words.d: the tendency of an object to keep its motion the same; more mass means more inertia
a force between two surfaces that rub together; it always works against motion

look.title: Newton States the First Law
look.text: In his 1687 book, the Principia, Newton wrote his first law in Latin. In an early English translation it says, roughly, that every body keeps its state of rest or of steady motion in a straight line, unless it is made to change that state by forces pressed upon it.
look.cite: Isaac Newton, Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica, 1687 (paraphrased from the 1729 English translation)
look.prompt: Newton says motion changes only when a force is 'pressed upon' the body. What force is pressed upon a rolling ball that slows to a stop on grass?

check.q: A ball rolls across a gym floor and slowly stops. What stopped it?
choices: Friction between the ball and the floor
check.why: Objects do not run out of force. A force, friction, acted against the motion and slowed the ball.

check.q: A spacecraft far from any planet turns off its engine. What happens to its motion?
choices: It keeps moving at the same speed in a straight line
It turns around and comes back
check.why: With almost no friction or gravity there, no net force acts, so its motion stays the same. That is the first law.

check.q: A bus stops suddenly and riders lurch forward. Which idea explains this best?
choices: Inertia: their bodies keep moving until a force stops them
Gravity pulls them toward the front
Friction from the seat pushes them forward
check.why: The bus stops, but the riders' bodies keep moving forward until a seat belt or something else supplies a stopping force.

lessons.title: Force, Mass and Acceleration
lessons.mainIdea: Newton's second law: a net force makes an object accelerate, and the acceleration is bigger with more force and smaller with more mass.
reading: Push an empty shopping cart and it speeds up quickly. Push a full one with the same effort and it speeds up slowly. Any change in speed or direction is called *acceleration*. Speeding up, slowing down and turning are all accelerations. A net force causes acceleration, and the amount depends on two things: how big the force is and how much *mass* the object has.

Newton's second law puts it in one line: force equals mass times acceleration, or F = m × a. Double the net force on the same cart and it accelerates twice as fast. Double the mass and push with the same force, and the acceleration is cut in half. Mass is the amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms. It does not change when you move to the Moon, even though weight does.

The units fit together. One newton is the force that gives one kilogram an acceleration of one meter per second every second. A 1,000-kilogram car that goes from 0 to 10 meters per second in 5 seconds accelerates at 2 meters per second per second. The net force on it must be about 2,000 newtons. If the engine pushes harder than that, friction and air are eating the difference.

The second law also explains slowing down. Brakes on a bike put a backward force on the wheels, so the bike accelerates backward, which we call decelerating. A heavier bike with the same brakes takes longer to stop. That is why loaded trucks need much longer stopping distances than cars, and why highway signs warn about it.

words.d: any change in speed or direction; speeding up, slowing down and turning all count
the amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms; it stays the same everywhere

look.title: Force Needed for the Same Acceleration
look.prompt: The mass goes from 1 kilogram to 10 kilograms. What happens to the force needed for the same acceleration, and what pattern do you see?

check.q: You push a 2-kilogram box and a 4-kilogram box with the same net force. Which accelerates more?
check.why: With the same force, less mass means more acceleration. Acceleration equals force divided by mass.

check.q: Which of these is an example of acceleration?
choices: A car turning a corner at a steady 20 miles per hour
A train moving at a constant speed on a straight track
A book resting on a shelf
A puck gliding on frictionless ice
check.why: Turning changes direction, and any change in speed or direction is acceleration. The others have no change.

check.q: A net force of 10 newtons acts on a 5-kilogram sled. What is its acceleration?
check.why: Acceleration equals force divided by mass: 10 divided by 5 is 2 meters per second per second.

lessons.title: Every Push Pushes Back
lessons.mainIdea: Newton's third law: forces come in pairs, so when one object pushes on another, the second pushes back equally hard in the opposite direction.
reading: Stand on a skateboard and push a wall. You roll backward. You pushed the wall, but the wall pushed you too. Newton's third law says forces always come in pairs. When object A pushes on object B, object B pushes back on object A with the same size force in the opposite direction. There is no such thing as a one-sided push.

This law confuses people, because it sounds like the two forces should cancel. They do not cancel, because they act on different objects. Your push acts on the wall. The wall's push acts on you. The wall is attached to the building, so it barely moves. You are on wheels, so you roll. Each object responds to the net force on itself.

A rocket works this way. The engine pushes hot gas downward out of the nozzle. The gas pushes the rocket upward. A swimmer pushes the water backward with her hands, and the water pushes her forward. When you walk, your foot pushes the ground backward, and the ground pushes you forward. On ice, your foot slips instead of pushing, so the ground cannot push you.

Even gravity comes in pairs. Earth pulls you down with your weight. You pull Earth up with exactly the same force. Earth has so much more mass that its acceleration toward you is far too small to notice, while your acceleration toward it is the familiar fall. Same force, very different masses, very different motions.

words.d: the two equal and opposite forces that two objects put on each other
the narrow opening at the back of a rocket engine where hot gas shoots out

look.title: Two Carts, One Spring
look.text: Two lab carts face each other on a track. A compressed spring is between them. Cart A has a mass of 1 kilogram. Cart B is loaded with extra weights to 3 kilograms. A student trips the spring. The spring pushes on both carts with the same force at the same time. Cart A shoots off at a high speed. Cart B moves off the other way, but at only one third of Cart A's speed.
look.prompt: The spring pushed on both carts equally. Use the second and third laws together to explain why the carts moved at different speeds.

check.q: A swimmer pushes water backward with her hands. What pushes her forward?
choices: Her own muscles pushing on her body
The water pushing forward on her hands
Gravity pulling her along the pool
check.why: Forces come in pairs. She pushes the water backward, and the water pushes her forward with an equal force.

check.q: Why do the two forces in a force pair not cancel each other out?
choices: Because they happen at different times
Because they act on two different objects
Because friction removes one of them
check.why: Each force acts on a different object, so each object feels only one of them. Forces cancel only when they act on the same object.

check.q: A rocket engine pushes hot gas downward. According to the third law, what happens?
choices: The gas pushes the rocket upward
The gas pulls the rocket downward
The rocket stays still until the air pushes it
The gas cancels the rocket's weight
check.why: The rocket pushes the gas down, so the gas pushes the rocket up with an equal force. That push lifts the rocket.

lessons.title: Why a Sudden Stop Hurts
lessons.mainIdea: Stopping a moving object takes force, and the faster it stops, the bigger the force must be.
reading: Catch a fast baseball with a stiff, straight arm and it stings. Catch it while letting your hand move back with the ball, and it does not. The ball loses the same motion either way. The difference is time. When the stop takes longer, the force can be smaller. When the stop is almost instant, the force must be huge.

The second law explains why. To stop an object, you must give it an acceleration backward. A quick stop is a big acceleration, and a big acceleration needs a big force. A slow stop is a small acceleration, so it needs only a small force. Engineers say the *impact* force depends on how long the *collision* lasts.

Think about the two eggs from the story. The taped egg hit hard tile and stopped in about a thousandth of a second. Maya's egg stopped over a much longer time as the straws bent and the cup crumpled. Both eggs lost all their downward motion, but the force on Maya's egg was far smaller, so its shell held.

The same thinking is everywhere. You bend your knees when you jump down from a step. Gymnasts land on thick mats. A car's front end is built to fold. In every case the goal is the same. Make the stop take longer, so the force stays small enough to be safe.

words.d: an event where two objects hit each other and push on each other for a short time
the moment and force of one object hitting another

look.title: The Same Jump, Two Landings
look.text: A gymnast jumps off a box onto a hard wooden floor and lands with straight, stiff legs. The stop is fast and jarring, and her knees ache. She jumps off the same box again, but this time she lands on a thick foam mat and lets her knees bend deeply. She sinks into the mat over a longer time and feels almost nothing. In both jumps she was moving at the same speed when her feet first touched down.
look.prompt: Both landings brought the gymnast to a stop from the same speed. Explain, using force and time, why the second landing felt so much gentler.

check.q: Why does a gymnast land on a thick foam mat instead of a bare floor?
choices: The mat makes her stop take longer, so the force is smaller
The mat makes her fall more slowly through the air
The mat cancels gravity while she lands
check.why: The mat stretches out the stopping time. A longer stop means a smaller acceleration and a smaller force on her body.

check.q: Two identical eggs fall from the same height. Egg A stops in 0.001 seconds on tile. Egg B stops in 0.1 seconds in foam. Which egg feels the bigger force?
choices: Egg B, because foam pushes harder
Egg A, because it stops in less time
check.why: Both lose the same motion, but Egg A does it in far less time. A faster stop needs a much bigger force.

check.q: You catch a hard-thrown ball. What should you do to reduce the sting?
choices: Push your hand toward the ball
Let your hand move back with the ball as you catch it
check.why: Moving your hand back makes the stop take longer, which lowers the force on your hand.

lessons.title: Helmets, Belts and Crumple Zones
lessons.mainIdea: Safety gear is designed to make a collision last longer and spread the force out, so the force on any one part of the body is smaller.
reading: A bike helmet looks like a hard shell, but the important part is the foam inside. In a crash, the foam crushes. Crushing takes time, and that time is the whole point. The head stops over a longer stretch instead of all at once, so the force on the skull and brain is much smaller. A helmet that has crushed once has done its job and should be replaced.

Cars use the same idea on a bigger scale. The front and back of a modern car are built as *crumple zones*: parts designed to fold up in a crash. That folding takes time and absorbs energy. The passenger area is built stiff so it keeps its shape. The car is wrecked on purpose so the people inside are not.

A seat belt supplies the stopping force from the first law. Without it, the car stops but you keep moving until you hit the dashboard, a very fast stop. A belt starts slowing you as soon as the car slows, and it spreads the force over your hips and chest. An *airbag* inflates in a fraction of a second and gives your head a soft, longer stop.

Engineers test these designs with crash test dummies full of sensors, then change the design and test again. The numbers guide each choice. The goal is never to make the crash disappear; that is impossible. The goal is to stretch it out and spread it around so the forces stay below what a body can take.

words.d: a part of a car built to fold up in a crash so the stop takes longer
a bag that inflates very fast in a crash to give the head a softer, longer stop

look.title: The Head and the Helmet
look.text: A student drops a melon from a ladder onto concrete. It splits open. She drops a second melon of the same size from the same height, but this one is strapped inside a bike helmet. The helmet's foam liner cracks and crushes on impact, but the melon inside has only a small bruise. She notices that the crushed helmet foam does not spring back; it stays dented.
look.prompt: The foam crushed and stayed dented. Why is foam that crushes better at protecting a head than a hard shell alone that does not bend at all?

check.q: What does the foam in a bike helmet do during a crash?
choices: It crushes so the head stops over a longer time
It bounces the head back safely
check.why: Crushing foam stretches the stopping time, which lowers the force on the head. That is the helmet's main job.

check.q: Why is the front of a car designed to crumple in a crash?
choices: To make the stop longer and absorb energy before it reaches the passengers
To keep the engine from getting wet
check.why: The crumple zone folds up over time, so the passenger area, built stiff, stops more gently.

check.q: In a crash without a seat belt, what stops the rider's forward motion?
choices: Nothing; the rider keeps moving forever
The dashboard or windshield, very suddenly
check.why: The rider keeps moving until something supplies a force. Without a belt, that something is the inside of the car, and the stop is fast and harmful.

lessons.title: Planning a Fair Test
lessons.mainIdea: A fair test changes only one variable at a time, keeps everything else the same, and repeats trials so the result can be trusted.
reading: Suppose you want to know whether a bigger parachute makes an egg land more gently. You could just try it once and see. But a single drop can go wrong for many reasons: a gust of air, a crooked release, a soft spot in the box. Scientists and engineers plan a *fair test* so the answer comes from the thing they changed and not from luck.

A fair test starts with one *variable*, the thing you choose to change. Here it is parachute size. Everything else must stay the same: the egg, the cup, the drop height, the floor, the way you let go. Those are the *controls*. If you changed the parachute and the drop height at the same time, you could not tell which one mattered.

Next you decide what to measure. 'Landed gently' is a feeling, not a measurement. Better choices are the time the fall takes, whether the egg cracks, or the dent left in a clay pad under the target. A phone's slow-motion video can count frames. Numbers let two people compare results and agree.

Finally, repeat. Three drops per parachute size is better than one, and five is better than three. If the big parachute wins every time, the pattern is real. If it wins once and loses twice, the parachute size may not matter as much as you thought, and that is a useful discovery too.

words.d: the one thing you change on purpose in a test to see what it does
the things you keep the same in a test so they cannot affect the result
a test that changes one variable, keeps the rest the same and repeats trials

look.title: Three Teams, Three Plans
look.text: Team 1 drops one egg from the top step with a small bag, then one from the middle step with a big bag. Team 2 drops three eggs with a small bag and three with a big bag, all from the top step, and times each fall with slow-motion video. Team 3 drops one egg with a big bag from the top step and declares that big bags always work best.
look.prompt: Which team ran a fair test? Name one thing each of the other two teams did that makes their conclusion hard to trust.

check.q: You want to test whether straw legs make an egg lander safer. Which is the best plan?
choices: Change the legs and the drop height together
Drop it once with legs and see what happens
Drop the same lander several times with legs and several times without, everything else the same
Ask other teams which design they like
check.why: A fair test changes one variable, keeps controls the same and repeats trials so the result is not luck.

check.q: In a test of parachute size, what is the variable?
choices: The floor the egg lands on
check.why: The variable is the one thing you change on purpose. Everything else, including height, egg and floor, is a control.

check.q: Why do scientists repeat a trial several times?
choices: So a single lucky or unlucky result does not fool them
Because the first trial never counts
Because one variable must be changed each time
check.why: Repeating shows whether the pattern is real or just chance. One drop can go wrong for many reasons.

lessons.title: Weight Is a Force
lessons.mainIdea: Weight is the force of gravity on an object's mass, so mass stays the same everywhere but weight changes from planet to planet.
reading: Drop a pencil. It falls. Gravity is a pull between any two objects that have mass. Earth is enormous, so its pull on you is strong enough to feel every second of your life. Your *weight* is the force of Earth's gravity pulling on your mass. Like every force, it is measured in newtons and has a direction: toward the center of Earth.

Mass and weight get mixed up, but they are different. Mass is how much matter you contain, and it does not change. Weight is a force, and it depends on where you are. Near Earth's surface, gravity pulls on every kilogram with about 9.8 newtons. A 50-kilogram student weighs about 490 newtons here. On the Moon, the pull is only about one sixth as strong, so the same student weighs about 80 newtons but still has a mass of 50 kilograms.

Gravity also gives all falling objects the same acceleration when air is not in the way: about 9.8 meters per second every second near Earth's surface. Drop a hammer and a feather in a room and the feather drifts down, because air pushes on it. In 1971, an Apollo astronaut dropped a hammer and a feather on the airless Moon. They hit the ground together.

That result matches Newton's second law. Gravity pulls harder on the hammer, but the hammer also has more mass and more inertia. The bigger force and the bigger mass balance out exactly, so the acceleration is the same. Galileo argued this in the 1600s using ramps and careful timing, long before anyone could test it in a vacuum.

words.d: the force of gravity pulling on an object; it changes from place to place
the pull between any two objects that have mass; Earth's pull holds us down

look.title: How Hard Gravity Pulls on 1 Kilogram
look.prompt: A 10-kilogram backpack has the same mass on every world. About how much would it weigh on Mars, and would it be easier or harder to lift than on Earth?

check.q: An astronaut with a mass of 70 kilograms travels to the Moon. What changes?
choices: Her mass drops to about 12 kilograms
Her weight drops, but her mass stays 70 kilograms
Both her mass and weight stay the same
Her mass drops, but her weight stays the same
check.why: Mass is the amount of matter and does not change. Weight is the pull of gravity, and the Moon pulls less.

check.q: A hammer and a feather are dropped together on the airless Moon. What happens?
choices: They land at the same time
check.why: Without air, gravity gives every object the same acceleration, so they fall together. Apollo astronauts showed this in 1971.

check.q: Gravity pulls harder on a bowling ball than on a marble. Why do they fall with the same acceleration?
choices: Air pushes up harder on the bowling ball
Gravity only pulls on heavy things
The bowling ball's greater mass needs a bigger force for the same acceleration
check.why: The bigger pull on the bowling ball is exactly matched by its bigger mass, so the acceleration, force divided by mass, comes out the same.

lessons.title: Mass, Distance and Orbits
lessons.mainIdea: The pull of gravity gets stronger with more mass and weaker with more distance, and that pull is what keeps moons and planets in their orbits.
reading: Every object with mass pulls on every other object. You pull on your desk and your desk pulls on you. You never notice, because the force is tiny. Gravity only becomes obvious when at least one of the objects is huge, like a planet. Two things set the strength of the pull: the masses involved and the *distance* between them.

More mass means more pull. Jupiter has far more mass than Earth, so its surface gravity is much stronger. More distance means less pull, and the drop-off is steep. Newton worked out that if you double the distance between two objects, the pull becomes only one fourth as strong. Triple the distance, and it is one ninth. That is why astronauts far from Earth feel almost nothing.

Gravity does not only pull things down. It also bends paths. The Moon is always falling toward Earth, but it is also moving sideways fast. The sideways motion and the downward pull combine into a curved path. That path never reaches the ground. It is an *orbit*. Newton imagined a cannonball fired from a mountaintop so fast that the ground curved away beneath it. That is exactly what a satellite does.

The same law reaches from a falling apple to the planets circling the Sun. Newton's idea was bold. The force that drops an apple and the force that holds the Moon are one and the same. That single rule let astronomers predict eclipses. It helped them find new planets from the wobbles of known ones. It guides spacecraft to the Moon and Mars today.

words.d: how far apart two objects are; gravity weakens quickly as distance grows
the curved path of an object that keeps falling toward a planet or star while moving sideways

look.title: Newton's Mountain
look.text: Picture a cannon on a mountain so tall it stands above the air. Fire a ball slowly, and it falls to the ground a short way off. Fire it faster, and it lands farther away, because Earth's surface curves down and away as the ball falls. Fire it fast enough, and the ground curves away just as fast as the ball drops. The ball never lands. It circles all the way around and comes back to the mountain from behind.
look.prompt: The cannonball in orbit is still falling the whole time. What keeps it from ever hitting the ground, and what would happen if gravity suddenly switched off?

check.q: Two objects are moved so they are twice as far apart. What happens to the gravitational pull between them?
choices: It becomes one fourth as strong
check.why: Gravity weakens with the square of the distance. Double the distance, and the pull drops to one fourth.

check.q: Why does the Moon not fall into Earth even though gravity pulls it?
choices: The Moon is too far away for gravity to reach it
The Moon's sideways motion combines with the pull to make a curved orbit
Earth and the Moon push each other apart
check.why: The Moon is falling toward Earth, but it moves sideways fast enough that its path curves around Earth instead of hitting it.

check.q: Which change would make the pull of gravity between two objects stronger?
choices: Making them both smaller in mass
Increasing the mass of one of them
check.why: More mass means a stronger pull. Distance works the other way: more distance means less pull.

lessons.title: Electric Charge at a Distance
lessons.mainIdea: Electric forces come from charge; like charges push apart, opposite charges pull together, and the force acts without touching.
reading: Rub a balloon on your hair and hold it near the wall. It sticks. Hold it near a thin stream of water from a faucet, and the stream bends toward the balloon. Nothing is touching the water. A force is reaching across the gap. This is an *electric force*, and it comes from *charge*.

Everything is made of atoms, and atoms contain tiny particles with charge. Protons carry positive charge and electrons carry negative charge. Most objects have equal amounts and act neutral. Rubbing can move some electrons from one object to another. The balloon gains extra electrons and becomes negative. Your hair loses them and becomes positive.

Charges follow a simple rule: opposites attract, and likes repel. The negative balloon pulls on the positive hair, which is why hair stands up toward it. Two rubbed balloons push each other apart. The force is stronger when the charges are bigger and weaker when they are farther apart, much like gravity, but electric forces can push as well as pull.

Scientists describe the space around a charge as an *electric field*. It is the region where any other charge would feel a force. The field is strongest near the charge and fades with distance. You cannot see a field, but you can map it. Move a small test charge around and record the push or pull at each spot. Lightning, static shocks and the touch screen on a phone all work by electric force.

words.d: a property of matter that causes electric force; it can be positive or negative
the push or pull between charged objects; opposites attract and likes repel
the space around a charge where another charge would feel a force

look.title: The Bending Stream
look.text: A student turns the faucet on to a thin, smooth stream. She rubs a balloon on her sweater for ten seconds and slowly brings it toward the water without touching it. The stream bends toward the balloon by about a centimeter. She moves the balloon closer and the bend grows. She touches the balloon to a metal sink, brings it back, and now the stream does not bend at all.
look.prompt: Why did the stream stop bending after the balloon touched the metal sink? What must have happened to the balloon's charge?

check.q: A rubbed balloon sticks to a wall without touching anything sticky. What holds it there?
choices: Electric force between the charged balloon and the wall
Air pressure pushing it against the wall
check.why: The charged balloon pulls on charges in the wall. That electric attraction reaches across the gap and holds it.

check.q: Two balloons are both rubbed on the same sweater. What happens when they are brought close?
check.why: Both gain the same kind of charge, and like charges repel each other.

check.q: What happens to the electric force between two charges as they move farther apart?
choices: It changes from a pull to a push
check.why: Like gravity, electric force fades with distance. Farther apart means a weaker push or pull.

lessons.title: Magnets, Fields and Electromagnets
lessons.mainIdea: Magnets push and pull through space using fields, and an electric current makes a magnetic field too, which lets us build electromagnets we can switch on and off.
reading: Hold two magnets near each other and you feel them pull or push before they touch. Every magnet has two ends called *poles*, north and south. Opposite poles attract and like poles repel. The space around a magnet where these forces act is its *magnetic field*. Sprinkle iron filings on paper over a magnet, and they line up in curves that show the field's shape.

For a long time, people thought electricity and magnetism were separate. In 1820, a Danish scientist named Hans Christian Oersted noticed that a compass needle swung when he switched on an electric current in a nearby wire. Moving charge makes a magnetic field. That discovery joined two sciences into one and made the modern world possible.

Wrap a wire into a coil, run a current through it, and you have an *electromagnet*. Add an iron core, and it gets much stronger. Unlike a bar magnet, you can switch it off, and you can make it stronger with more coils or more current. Scrap yards use giant electromagnets to lift cars. Electric motors, speakers, doorbells and the drive of a Chicago 'L' train all use them.

Fields explain how forces act without touching. Earth itself is a giant magnet, and a compass needle lines up with its field. That is why a hiker in a forest preserve outside Chicago can find north with a needle that has no idea where it is. Gravity, electricity and magnetism all reach across empty space in this way: through fields.

words.d: the two ends of a magnet, north and south; opposite poles attract and like poles repel
the space around a magnet or a current where magnetic forces act
a coil of wire that becomes a magnet when current flows, and stops when it is off

look.title: A Compass Needle Moves
look.text: In a short report published in 1820, Oersted described placing a straight wire above a compass needle and connecting the wire to a battery. The moment the current flowed, the needle swung to the side. When he reversed the current, the needle swung the other way. He concluded that an electric current produces a magnetic effect in the space around the wire.
look.cite: Hans Christian Oersted, report on the effect of electric current on a magnetic needle, 1820 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Oersted's needle moved without anything touching it. What does this tell you about the space around a wire carrying current?

check.q: What did Oersted discover in 1820?
choices: That an electric current makes a magnetic field
That Earth has no magnetic field
check.why: His compass needle swung when current flowed in a nearby wire, showing that moving charge creates a magnetic field.

check.q: Which is an advantage of an electromagnet over a bar magnet?
choices: It can be switched off and its strength can be changed
It is always stronger than any bar magnet
check.why: Current makes the field, so cutting the current turns the magnet off. More coils or more current make it stronger.

check.q: Iron filings sprinkled near a magnet line up in curved patterns. What do the patterns show?
choices: The heat given off by the magnet
The electric charge on the magnet
The shape of the magnetic field around it
check.why: Each filing becomes a tiny magnet and lines up with the field, so the pattern traces the invisible field's shape.

review.q: A box is pushed with 25 newtons to the right and 25 newtons to the left. What happens to its motion?
review.why: Equal and opposite forces give a net force of zero, and zero net force means no change in motion.

review.q: Which law explains why a rider lurches forward when a bus brakes?
choices: The rule that like charges repel
review.why: The rider's body keeps moving at the bus's old speed until a force, such as a seat belt, changes that motion.

review.q: A net force of 20 newtons acts on a 4-kilogram wagon. What is its acceleration?
review.why: Acceleration equals force divided by mass: 20 divided by 4 is 5 meters per second per second.

review.q: You push on a wall while wearing roller skates and roll backward. What pushed you?
choices: The wall, with a force equal to your push
review.why: Forces come in pairs. You pushed the wall, and the wall pushed back on you just as hard in the opposite direction.

review.q: Why does a crumple zone make a car crash safer for the people inside?
choices: It makes the car stop faster
It makes the stop take longer, so the force on the passengers is smaller
It keeps the car from moving at all
review.why: Folding metal stretches the stopping time, and a longer stop means a smaller acceleration and a smaller force.

review.q: A student tests whether a bigger parachute slows an egg lander. What must she keep the same?
choices: The drop height, the egg and the lander design
Nothing; changing everything gives more data
Only the color of the parachute
review.why: In a fair test, only the variable changes. Everything else is a control so the result comes from the parachute size alone.

review.q: A rock has a mass of 6 kilograms on Earth. What is its mass on the Moon?
review.why: Mass is the amount of matter and never changes with location. Only the weight, the pull of gravity, changes.

review.q: Which statement about fields is correct?
choices: Fields only exist inside solid objects
Only magnets have fields; gravity and charge do not
A field is a kind of visible light around an object
A field is the region around an object where its force can act on other objects without touching
review.why: Gravity, electric and magnetic forces all reach across space through fields, which grow weaker with distance.

chapters.title: Energy: Kinetic, Potential and Heat
chapters.bigQuestion: Where does the energy of a moving, falling or warming object come from, and where does it go?

story.title: The First Hill
story.kicker: A chain hauls the train up. After that, no motor touches it until the ride is over.
paragraphs: On a July morning in Gurnee, Illinois, about an hour north of Chicago, the gates of Six Flags Great America open and a crowd runs for the coasters. Jamal and his cousin Rosa get in line for the tallest one they can find. From the ground, its first hill looks like a wall of steel. They watch a train crawl up it, slow as a bicycle, and then drop out of sight with a roar and a chorus of screams.

Their turn comes. The lap bar clicks down. The train rolls out of the station and catches a chain that clanks under the track. For a long, slow minute the chain drags them upward. Rosa notices that nothing about this part is exciting. It is a machine doing work, lifting the train and every rider in it higher and higher above the parking lot.

At the top, the chain lets go. For a moment the train barely moves. Then the front cars tip over the edge, and the whole train falls. The wind tears at Jamal's face. The ground rushes up. At the bottom of the drop they are moving faster than a car on the highway, and the train flies up the second hill without any motor pushing it at all.

Hill after hill, the pattern repeats. Each climb is a little lower than the one before. Each drop is a little slower. By the final turn, the train is coasting, and brakes squeeze the rails to bring it into the station. Rosa's hair is a mess and Jamal is laughing. The ride lasted two minutes, and a motor only worked for the first one.

Later, waiting for funnel cake, Rosa asks the question this chapter answers. The chain gave the train one push, up the first hill. Where did the speed for every drop after that come from? Why was each hill lower than the last? And where did all that motion go when the train finally stopped, with the brakes warm to the touch?
story.think: The train's motor only worked during the slow climb up the first hill. Where was the energy for the rest of the ride stored, and what clue tells you some of it was lost along the way?

lessons.title: Kinetic Energy Grows with Speed
lessons.mainIdea: Kinetic energy is the energy of motion; it grows with mass and grows even faster with speed, because speed is squared.
reading: A moving bowling ball can knock down pins. A moving hammer can drive a nail. Anything that moves carries *energy*, the ability to make something happen: to push, to lift, to heat, to break. The energy of motion is called *kinetic energy*. The unit of energy is the *joule*. Lifting an apple about one meter takes roughly one joule.

Two things set how much kinetic energy an object has. The first is mass. A loaded truck at 30 miles per hour has far more kinetic energy than a bicycle at 30 miles per hour, and that is why it does far more damage in a crash. Double the mass at the same speed and you double the kinetic energy.

The second is speed, and speed counts more than mass. Kinetic energy depends on speed multiplied by itself, the speed squared. Double the speed and the kinetic energy becomes four times bigger. Triple the speed and it becomes nine times bigger. That is why a car at 60 miles per hour needs about four times the stopping distance of the same car at 30, not twice.

You can test this with a ball and a cup on a table. Roll a ball slowly into a paper cup and the cup slides a little. Roll it twice as fast and the cup slides about four times as far. The distance the cup moves is a way to measure how much energy the ball delivered. More speed means much more energy to hand over.

words.d: the ability to make something happen: to move, lift, heat or change an object
the energy an object has because it is moving
the unit of energy; lifting an apple one meter takes about one joule

look.title: Kinetic Energy of a 1-Kilogram Ball
look.cite: computed from kinetic energy = one half × mass × speed squared
look.prompt: The speed goes from 1 to 2 meters per second and then to 4. How does the energy change each time the speed doubles?

check.q: A car's speed doubles from 20 to 40 miles per hour. What happens to its kinetic energy?
check.why: Kinetic energy depends on speed squared. Doubling the speed multiplies the energy by two times two, or four.

check.q: Which object has the most kinetic energy?
choices: A 1-kilogram ball rolling at 1 meter per second
A 1-kilogram ball rolling at 3 meters per second
A 2-kilogram ball rolling at 1 meter per second
check.why: Tripling the speed multiplies the energy by nine, which beats doubling the mass. The parked truck has no kinetic energy.

check.q: A ball rolled at twice the speed pushes a paper cup about four times as far. What does this show?
choices: Energy grows with the square of the speed
check.why: The cup's slide measures the energy delivered. Four times the slide at double the speed matches the speed-squared rule.

lessons.title: Stored Energy: Height, Springs and Fields
lessons.mainIdea: Potential energy is stored energy that depends on position, such as height above the ground, a stretched spring or charges held apart.
reading: A book on a high shelf is not moving, but it can still make something happen. Nudge it off and it falls, gaining speed and kinetic energy. The energy was there all along, stored by the book's position. Stored energy that depends on position is called *potential energy*. Lifting the book gave it energy; falling releases it.

The most familiar kind is *gravitational potential energy*. It grows with mass and with height. Lifting a 1-kilogram book 1 meter stores about 10 joules. Lift it 2 meters and it stores about 20. A roller coaster at the top of a 60-meter hill has a huge amount, and every bit of it came from the chain motor doing work on the train during the climb.

Springs and rubber bands store *elastic potential energy*. Stretch a bow, and the bent limbs hold energy until the string is released and the arrow flies. A trampoline stores your energy as the mat stretches downward and then gives it back as it snaps up. A wind-up toy stores energy in a coiled spring and lets it out slowly through gears.

Fields store energy too. Pull a magnet away from the refrigerator and you store energy that is released when it snaps back. Push two like charges together and they store energy that is released when they fly apart. Even food and fuel store energy in the electric forces between atoms, which is why chemists call it chemical potential energy.

words.d: stored energy that depends on the position or shape of an object
energy stored by lifting something higher; it grows with mass and height
energy stored in a stretched or squeezed object like a spring or rubber band

look.title: The Pendulum and the Nose
look.text: A teacher hangs a heavy bowling ball from the ceiling on a long rope. She stands against the wall, holds the ball right against her nose, and lets go without pushing it. The ball swings across the room, rises, stops, and swings back toward her face. She does not flinch. The ball stops just short of her nose and swings away again. Each swing it climbs a little less high than the time before.
look.prompt: Why is the teacher sure the ball cannot come back higher than her nose? What would change if she gave it a small push when she let go?

check.q: Which object has the most gravitational potential energy?
check.why: Gravitational potential energy grows with both mass and height, and the 2-kilogram book at 2 meters has the most of both.

check.q: A stretched bow is held ready to fire. What kind of energy does it hold?
choices: No energy until the arrow moves
check.why: The bent bow stores energy by its shape. When released, that stored energy becomes the arrow's kinetic energy.

check.q: Where did the potential energy of a roller coaster at the top of the first hill come from?
choices: From the wind at the top
From the chain motor lifting the train during the climb
check.why: The motor did work on the train, pulling it up against gravity. That work is now stored as height.

lessons.title: The Roller Coaster Trade
lessons.mainIdea: Energy is never created or destroyed; on a coaster, height turns into speed and back again, and friction slowly turns some of it into heat.
reading: At the top of the first hill, the train has lots of gravitational potential energy and almost no kinetic energy. As it drops, height is traded for speed. At the bottom, it has little potential energy and lots of kinetic energy. Up the second hill, speed is traded back for height. The total, potential plus kinetic, stays nearly the same all the way through. This is the law of *conservation of energy*. Energy changes form, but it does not vanish.

That law explains why every hill after the first must be lower. The train can only rise as high as its energy allows, and the first hill set that budget. If a second hill were taller than the first, the train would roll backward. Coaster designers use this rule for every hill, loop and turn, and they add a margin so a heavy train on a cold day still makes it over.

But the hills shrink faster than a perfect trade would predict. Each hill is lower than the last because some energy leaks away as *heat*. Wheels rub the rails. Air pushes against the cars. Bearings warm up. None of the energy is destroyed; it spreads into the track, the air and the metal as thermal energy, where it can no longer lift the train. At the end, the brakes turn all the remaining motion into heat, which is why they are warm.

James Joule proved the connection between motion and heat in the 1840s with a paddle wheel spinning in water. A falling weight turned the paddle, and the water warmed by a tiny, measurable amount. Motion was becoming heat, and the amount matched. His careful measurements helped convince scientists that energy in all its forms is one thing, counted in one unit that now bears his name.

words.d: the law that energy changes form but is never created or destroyed
energy moving from a warmer object to a cooler one

look.title: Joule on Energy That Does Not Vanish
look.text: In an 1847 public lecture in Manchester, Joule argued that when motion seems to disappear, as when a moving object is stopped by friction, it is not destroyed but turned into heat. He said that nature's store of energy is never lost, only changed from one form into another, and that the amount of heat produced always matches the motion that vanished.
look.cite: James Prescott Joule, lecture 'On Matter, Living Force, and Heat', Manchester, 1847 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Joule says motion stopped by friction becomes heat. Where on the roller coaster would you expect to find that heat at the end of the ride?

check.q: Why must every hill on a roller coaster be lower than the first hill?
choices: The train's energy budget was set by the first hill, and it loses some to friction after that
The chain only reaches the first hill
Taller hills would weigh too much
check.why: Energy is conserved, so the train cannot climb higher than its starting energy allows, and friction and air drain some away on every hill.

check.q: At the bottom of the first drop, what has happened to the train's energy?
choices: It has been destroyed by the fall
Most of the potential energy has become kinetic energy
Most of the kinetic energy has become potential energy
check.why: Falling trades height for speed. The total stays nearly the same, but the form changes from potential to kinetic.

check.q: What happened to the train's kinetic energy after the brakes stopped it?
choices: It went back into the chain motor
It became thermal energy in the brakes and rails
It became potential energy in the riders
check.why: The brakes used friction to turn motion into heat, which is why they are warm after a ride. The energy was not destroyed.

lessons.title: Temperature Is Not Heat
lessons.mainIdea: Temperature measures how fast particles move on average, while thermal energy is the total motion energy of all the particles in an object.
reading: Everything is made of particles too small to see, and they never stop moving. In a solid they jiggle in place. In a liquid they slide past each other. In a gas they zip around and bounce off the walls. The energy of all this motion, added up, is the object's *thermal energy*. Rub your hands together and they get warm because friction made their particles jiggle faster.

*Temperature* is different. It measures how fast the particles are moving on average, not how many there are. A thermometer reports the average, in degrees. Compare a cup of tea at 90 degrees Celsius with a bathtub of water at 40 degrees Celsius. The tea is hotter. But the tub holds far more water, so its total thermal energy is much larger.

A spark from a sparkler can be over 1,000 degrees Celsius, yet it does not burn you. It is tiny, so it carries very little total energy and cools in an instant. A pot of boiling water at 100 degrees Celsius is far more dangerous, because it holds a huge amount of thermal energy and can pour it into your skin. Temperature tells you how hot; thermal energy tells you how much.

Heat is the third word, and it is a verb as much as a noun. Heat is thermal energy on the move, flowing from a warmer object to a cooler one. When you hold a warm mug, heat flows into your hands. Hold an ice cube and heat flows out of your hand into the ice. The ice does not send cold into you; you send heat into it.

words.d: the total energy of motion of all the particles in an object
a measure of how fast the particles in an object move on average

look.title: The Cup and the Tub
look.text: A student pours a small cup of water at 80 degrees Celsius into a large tub of water at 20 degrees Celsius and stirs. The tub water warms by less than one degree. Then he pours a whole bucket of 80-degree water into the same tub and stirs again. This time the tub warms by several degrees. Both pours started at the same temperature.
look.prompt: The cup and the bucket had the same temperature. Why did the bucket change the tub so much more? Which one carried more thermal energy?

check.q: A sparkler spark is over 1,000 degrees Celsius but does not burn you. Why?
choices: The spark is so tiny it carries very little total thermal energy
check.why: Temperature is high, but the amount of matter is tiny, so the total thermal energy is very small and cools instantly.

check.q: Which best describes temperature?
choices: The total energy in an object
A measure of the average motion of an object's particles
The amount of heat an object gives off
The weight of the particles in an object
check.why: Temperature is an average of how fast particles move. Total energy also depends on how much matter there is.

check.q: You hold an ice cube and your hand feels cold. What is happening?
choices: Cold flows from the ice into your hand
Nothing flows; your hand just senses the ice
Heat flows from your hand into the ice
The ice absorbs the temperature of your hand
check.why: Heat always flows from warmer to cooler. Your warm hand loses thermal energy to the ice, and that loss feels cold.

lessons.title: Heat Flows Hot to Cold
lessons.mainIdea: Heat always flows from a warmer object to a cooler one until they reach the same temperature, and friction is one way to make it.
reading: Put a cold spoon into hot soup. The spoon warms and the soup cools a tiny bit. Leave them long enough and they reach the same temperature. Heat flows on its own in only one direction: from hot to cold. It never flows from a cold spoon into hotter soup by itself. When two objects reach the same temperature, the flow stops, and we say they are in *thermal equilibrium*.

Why one direction? Picture the fast-jiggling particles of the soup bumping the slow ones in the spoon. On average, the fast ones lose a little speed in each bump and the slow ones gain a little. Energy spreads out from where it is concentrated to where it is not. It would take an outside push, like a refrigerator's motor, to move heat the other way.

In 1798, an American-born scientist working in Germany, Benjamin Thompson, known as Count Rumford, watched cannon barrels being drilled. The metal got hot enough to boil water, and it kept getting hot as long as the drill kept turning. Most scientists then thought heat was an invisible fluid stored in matter. Rumford argued that a fluid would run out; the drilling did not. He concluded that heat was being made by motion.

Rumford's cannon and Joule's paddle wheel point at the same idea from two directions. Rub, drill, stir or brake, and you turn motion into thermal energy. That energy then flows from the warm spot outward into cooler surroundings. This is why a drill bit gets too hot to touch, why brakes glow on a mountain road, and why a meteor streaking through the air burns bright.

words.d: the state where two objects have reached the same temperature and heat stops flowing between them
a material that slows the flow of heat, such as foam, wool or still air

look.title: Rumford at the Cannon Foundry
look.text: In his 1798 paper to the Royal Society, Rumford described drilling a cannon barrel with a dull tool while the barrel sat in a box of water. After about two and a half hours, the water boiled. He noted that the heat seemed to have no limit as long as the drilling continued, and he argued that anything a body could keep supplying without end could not be a substance, so heat must be a kind of motion.
look.cite: Benjamin Thompson, Count Rumford, 'An Experimental Enquiry Concerning the Source of the Heat which is Excited by Friction', Philosophical Transactions, 1798 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Rumford's key evidence was that the heat never ran out. Why would that be a problem for the idea that heat is a fluid stored inside the metal?

check.q: A warm can of soda is placed in a bucket of ice water. What happens?
choices: Cold flows from the water into the soda
Heat flows from the soda into the water until they match in temperature
Heat flows from the water into the soda
Nothing happens until the ice melts
check.why: Heat flows from warmer to cooler on its own. The soda loses thermal energy to the ice water until both reach the same temperature.

check.q: What did Rumford observe that made him doubt heat was a stored fluid?
choices: The cannon got cold when drilled
The water in the box turned to ice
The heat from drilling never ran out as long as the drill turned
The drill stopped working after an hour
check.why: A stored fluid would eventually be used up. Endless heat from continued motion suggested that motion itself was making the heat.

check.q: Two objects are in thermal equilibrium. What must be true?
choices: They have the same thermal energy
They have the same temperature and heat is no longer flowing between them
check.why: Equilibrium means the temperatures match. Their total thermal energy can still differ if their sizes differ.

lessons.title: Conduction Through Touching Things
lessons.mainIdea: Conduction is heat moving through a material by particles bumping their neighbors; metals conduct well, and foam, wool and air conduct poorly.
reading: Leave a metal spoon in a pot of hot soup and the handle soon burns your fingers. Leave a wooden spoon and the handle stays cool. Heat moved along the metal spoon by *conduction*: fast-moving particles at the hot end bump their neighbors, which bump theirs, passing the energy along the spoon without the particles moving far themselves.

Some materials pass this energy along quickly. Metals like copper and aluminum are excellent *conductors*. Their loose electrons help carry energy through the metal. Other materials pass it along slowly. Wood, plastic, foam, wool and glass are poor conductors. We call a poor conductor an insulator. Still air is one of the best insulators of all. That is why fluffy materials full of air pockets keep you warm.

Conduction explains why a metal railing feels colder than a wooden one on a winter morning, even though both are the same temperature. The metal pulls heat out of your hand fast, so your skin cools and reports cold. The wood pulls heat slowly, so your skin stays warm. Your hand is measuring how fast heat leaves, not how cold the object is.

Engineers choose materials for conduction on purpose. Pot bottoms are copper or aluminum to move heat into food quickly. Pot handles are plastic or wood to keep it away from your hand. A winter coat traps air. A foam cooler is mostly trapped gas bubbles. In every case, the question is the same: do you want heat to move fast or slow?

words.d: heat moving through a material as particles bump their neighbors
a material that lets heat move through it quickly, such as copper or aluminum

look.title: Two Railings, One Morning
look.text: On a cold January morning in Chicago, a student touches a steel railing and then a wooden bench beside it. The steel feels bitterly cold. The wood feels merely cool. She checks both with an infrared thermometer. Both read the same temperature, minus 5 degrees Celsius. She tries the test again with a gloved hand and cannot tell the two apart.
look.prompt: Both objects were the same temperature. Why did the steel feel so much colder, and why did the glove erase the difference?

check.q: Why does a metal spoon in hot soup get hot along its handle?
choices: Hot soup climbs up the spoon
Heat moves along the metal by conduction as particles bump their neighbors
The air around the spoon heats it
check.why: In conduction, energy passes from particle to particle through the material. Metals do this very quickly.

check.q: Which material is the best insulator?
check.why: Foam holds many pockets of still air, and air is a very poor conductor of heat.

check.q: A steel railing and a wooden bench are both at minus 5 degrees Celsius. Why does the steel feel colder?
choices: Steel pulls heat out of your hand much faster than wood does
Steel is actually colder than wood
check.why: Your skin senses how fast it loses heat. Steel conducts heat away quickly, so it feels colder even at the same temperature.

lessons.title: Convection Moves the Fluid Itself
lessons.mainIdea: Convection carries heat by moving warm liquid or gas from place to place, driving everything from a boiling pot to the lake breeze in Chicago.
reading: Watch a pot of water on the stove just before it boils. Water at the bottom warms first, expands, and becomes a little less dense than the cooler water above it. So it rises. Cooler water sinks to take its place, warms, and rises in turn. This rolling loop is a *convection* current. Heat is carried by the moving water itself, not passed particle to particle.

Convection works in any fluid, which means any liquid or gas. Warm air from a heater rises to the ceiling while cool air slides along the floor, which is why your feet are the coldest part of a room. Smoke rises above a candle. A hawk circles without flapping inside a column of warm air rising from a sun-baked parking lot.

Chicago feels convection on a large scale. On a hot summer afternoon, the land warms faster than Lake Michigan, so air over the land rises. Cooler air from over the lake slides in to replace it, and the neighborhoods near the shore get a lake breeze that can be many degrees cooler than the suburbs. Weather forecasters for the city mention it all summer long.

Convection shapes the planet. Air warmed near the equator rises and moves toward the poles, driving winds. Ocean currents carry warm water from the tropics to cooler seas. Even Earth's interior churns by convection over millions of years, slowly moving the plates that carry the continents. The same loop in a soup pot is at work under your feet.

words.d: heat carried by the movement of a warm liquid or gas from one place to another
how much mass is packed into a given space; warm fluids are usually less dense and rise
anything that flows: a liquid or a gas

look.title: Colored Water in a Fish Tank
look.text: A class fills a clear tank with room-temperature water. They lower a small jar of hot water dyed red to the bottom on one side and a jar of ice-cold water dyed blue to the bottom on the other side, and gently pull off the lids. The red water rises in a plume toward the surface and spreads across the top. The blue water spills out and creeps along the bottom. After a few minutes the tank shows a slow loop: red across the top, blue along the bottom.
look.prompt: Why did the hot red water rise and the cold blue water stay low? What does this show about how heat moves in a lake or a room?

check.q: In a pot on the stove, why does the water at the bottom rise?
choices: It gets hot, expands and becomes less dense than the cooler water above
check.why: Heating makes the water expand and become less dense, so it floats upward while cooler, denser water sinks.

check.q: Why is the floor of a heated room usually cooler than the ceiling?
choices: Warm air rises and cool air sinks by convection
The floor absorbs cold from the ground
Cold air is lighter than warm air
check.why: Warm air is less dense and rises to the ceiling, while cooler, denser air settles near the floor.

check.q: What drives Chicago's summer lake breeze?
choices: The lake is warmer than the land
Warm air rising over the hot land pulls in cooler air from over the lake
check.why: The land heats faster than the lake, warm air over the land rises, and cooler lake air flows in to replace it. That is convection.

lessons.title: Radiation Needs No Matter
lessons.mainIdea: Radiation carries heat as invisible infrared light, which needs no material to travel through and can cross empty space.
reading: Stand near a campfire and your face feels warm even when the air between you and the fire is cool and the wind blows the other way. The heat is not conducted through the air, and it is not carried by rising air, because you are beside the fire, not above it. It arrives as *radiation*: waves of light, mostly a kind your eyes cannot see, called *infrared*.

Every object warmer than absolute zero gives off infrared radiation. Warmer objects give off more of it. Your body glows in infrared all the time, which is how a thermal camera can find a person in the dark. Hold your hand near a hot stove burner without touching it and you feel that glow directly. Very hot objects like the burner's coil also glow in visible red.

In 1800, the astronomer William Herschel spread sunlight into a rainbow with a prism and placed thermometers in each color. Red warmed the thermometer more than violet. Then he tried the dark space just beyond the red, where no color was visible. That thermometer warmed the most of all. He had found invisible light that carried heat: infrared.

Radiation is the only way heat can cross empty space. Conduction and convection both need matter. The Sun's energy reaches Earth this way, across about 150 million kilometers of nearly empty space. Dark, rough surfaces absorb radiation well. Shiny surfaces reflect it. That is why a black car seat gets hotter in the sun than a white one. It is also why a foil blanket keeps a runner warm.

words.d: heat carried by light waves, including invisible infrared, which can cross empty space
a kind of light your eyes cannot see that carries heat; warm objects give it off

look.title: Herschel's Thermometer Beyond the Red
look.text: In his 1800 paper, Herschel described passing sunlight through a prism and setting blackened thermometers in the colored bands. The temperature rose more toward the red end. When he moved a thermometer just past the red, into a region with no visible light, it rose higher still. He concluded that the Sun sends out invisible rays that heat objects, and that they obey the same laws of reflection and refraction as visible light.
look.cite: William Herschel, 'Experiments on the Refrangibility of the Invisible Rays of the Sun', Philosophical Transactions, 1800 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Herschel's thermometer warmed in a spot where he could see nothing. What did that tell him, and how could he be sure it was not just the warm room?

check.q: How does the Sun's energy reach Earth across empty space?
choices: By radiation, as light including infrared
check.why: Conduction and convection need matter. Only radiation, which travels as light, can cross empty space.

check.q: What did Herschel find just beyond the red end of the rainbow?
choices: A place that was colder than the colors
Invisible rays that warmed a thermometer more than any visible color
check.why: The thermometer past red warmed the most, revealing invisible infrared light that carries heat.

check.q: Which surface will get hottest sitting in direct sunlight?
check.why: Dark surfaces absorb most of the radiation that hits them, while shiny and white surfaces reflect much of it away.

lessons.title: Designing a Drink Keeper
lessons.mainIdea: To keep a drink hot or cold, a design must slow conduction, convection and radiation at the same time, and a fair test shows which design works best.
reading: A hot chocolate on a January morning in Chicago cools fast. Heat leaves the cup in all three ways. It conducts through the cup walls into the air and your hand. Rising warm air and steam carry it away by convection. And the cup's warm surface radiates infrared into the room. A good container fights all three at once, and the same design keeps a cold drink cold.

To slow conduction, surround the drink with an insulator: foam, cork, layers of paper, or a wall with a gap of still air. To stop convection, put on a lid so warm air cannot rise away and carry heat with it. To reduce radiation, use a shiny inner surface that reflects infrared back toward the drink. A vacuum flask does all three: two shiny walls with almost no air between them, plus a tight stopper.

Testing is where the science happens. Fill several containers with water at the same starting temperature. Put a thermometer in each. Record the temperature every five minutes for an hour. Keep everything else the same: the same amount of water, the same room, the same starting temperature. Then compare. The container whose water changed the least is the best insulator.

Real designs involve trade-offs. Thick foam insulates well but is bulky. A metal vacuum flask works best but costs more and can dent. A lid slows convection but makes drinking awkward. Engineers weigh cost, weight, size and how well it works. The data from a fair test tells them which trade is worth making.

words.d: a space with almost no air or other matter in it; heat cannot conduct or convect across it
giving up one good thing, like low cost, to get another, like better insulation

look.title: Four Cups, One Hour
look.text: A class fills four containers with hot water at 80 degrees Celsius: a paper cup with no lid, a paper cup with a lid, a foam cup with a lid, and a steel vacuum flask with a stopper. After one hour, the open paper cup reads 38 degrees, the lidded paper cup 46, the foam cup with lid 58, and the vacuum flask 76. The room stayed at 21 degrees the whole time.
look.prompt: Which single change, adding a lid or switching paper for foam, made the bigger difference, and which way of heat flow does each change fight?

check.q: Why does a lid help keep a drink hot?
choices: It stops warm air and steam from rising away by convection
It conducts heat back into the drink
check.why: Without a lid, warm air and steam carry heat away from the surface. A lid blocks that convection.

check.q: Which container design slows all three ways heat moves?
choices: A thin metal cup with no lid
A glass cup with a lid
A shiny double-walled flask with a vacuum between the walls and a stopper
A paper cup wrapped in foil
check.why: The vacuum blocks conduction and convection between the walls, the shiny surfaces reflect radiation, and the stopper blocks convection at the top.

check.q: In a fair test of drink containers, which must be kept the same?
choices: The starting temperature and amount of water
check.why: The container is the variable. The water amount, starting temperature and room are controls so the results can be compared fairly.

lessons.title: Calories Are Energy
lessons.mainIdea: Food stores chemical energy that your body releases to move, grow and stay warm, and the Calorie on a label is a unit of that energy.
reading: You are a machine that runs on stored energy. Every step, heartbeat and thought is powered by energy released from food. The energy is stored in the chemical bonds that hold food molecules together. When your body breaks those bonds and combines the pieces with oxygen, energy is released, and your body uses it or gives it off as heat.

Food labels measure this energy in *Calories*. One food Calorie is about 4,200 joules, enough to lift a small apple about four kilometers straight up. Different foods store different amounts. Fats hold about 9 Calories per gram. Carbohydrates and proteins hold about 4 Calories per gram. Water and fiber hold almost none, which is why a big salad has fewer Calories than a small handful of nuts.
