Scientists first measured food energy by burning it. A *calorimeter* is an insulated container where a sample burns and the heat released warms a known amount of water. Measure the temperature rise, and you know the energy. Your body does something like slow, controlled burning, without the flame, and ends up with the same energy total.

Where does the energy go? Some becomes the kinetic energy of your muscles. Some builds new tissue. A lot becomes heat, which is why a room full of people warms up and why you sweat on a run. Your body runs at about 37 degrees Celsius, and food is the fuel that keeps it there on a cold day.

words.d: the unit of food energy on labels; one Calorie is about 4,200 joules
an insulated device that measures energy by how much it warms a known amount of water
energy stored in the bonds between atoms in food, fuel and batteries

look.title: Energy Stored in Food, by Type
look.prompt: A 10-gram serving of oil and a 10-gram serving of sugar: about how many Calories does each hold, and which foods would you expect to be mostly water?

check.q: Where is the energy in food stored before you eat it?
choices: In the chemical bonds between its atoms
check.why: Food holds chemical potential energy in its bonds, released when your body breaks them down with oxygen.

check.q: Which has the most Calories?
check.why: Fat stores about 9 Calories per gram, more than twice the 4 Calories per gram in protein or carbohydrate.

check.q: How does a calorimeter measure the energy in a food sample?
choices: By weighing the food before and after
By measuring how much the food shrinks
By burning it and measuring how much a known amount of water warms
check.why: The heat from burning the sample raises the water temperature. The bigger the rise, the more energy the food held.

lessons.title: Fuels and Their Trade-offs
lessons.mainIdea: Fuels store chemical energy that we release as heat and motion, and every fuel choice involves trade-offs in cost, convenience and effects on the environment.
reading: Gasoline, natural gas, coal, wood and the batteries in a phone all store energy. Gasoline is the fuel in most cars. When it burns with oxygen in an engine, chemical energy becomes hot gas that pushes pistons and turns the wheels. A large share of that energy becomes waste heat out the tailpipe and radiator, which is why engines need cooling.

In Illinois, electricity comes from several sources. The state has more nuclear reactors than any other. It also burns natural gas and some coal. Wind farms across the prairie and solar panels add a growing share. Each source turns stored or moving energy into electric energy that reaches a wall outlet. There, a charger turns it into chemical energy stored in a battery.

No fuel is free of trade-offs. Coal and gasoline store a lot of energy in a small space and are easy to move. But burning them releases *carbon dioxide*, which traps heat in the atmosphere, along with other pollution. Wind and sunlight release no carbon dioxide while making power. But they depend on the weather and need batteries or other backup. Nuclear plants make steady power without carbon dioxide. But they leave waste that must be stored safely for a very long time.

Scientists measure what each source costs, how much energy it delivers, and what it leaves behind. Citizens and lawmakers decide how to weigh those numbers. Understanding energy transfer lets you read those debates with clear eyes. Every bit of energy at the outlet came from somewhere. It changed form several times, and it left a trail of heat behind.

words.d: a material that stores chemical energy we can release, usually by burning it
a gas released when fuels burn; it traps heat in the atmosphere

look.title: Three Ways to Heat a Kettle
look.text: Three families heat the same kettle of water on the same cold morning. One uses a gas stove, burning natural gas under the kettle. One uses an electric kettle plugged into a wall outlet in a city whose power comes mostly from nuclear and gas plants. One camps and boils the kettle over a wood fire. All three kettles reach 100 degrees Celsius. Each family notices something different: the gas bill, the electric bill, or the smoke and the pile of firewood that got smaller.
look.prompt: Trace the energy for each kettle back to where it was stored. What did each family give up, and what did each one leave behind?

check.q: What happens to the chemical energy in gasoline when a car engine burns it?
choices: It becomes kinetic energy of the car and a lot of waste heat
It becomes potential energy in the gas tank
check.why: Burning releases the stored energy as hot gas that moves the pistons. Much of it leaves as heat, which is why engines need cooling.

check.q: Which is a trade-off of wind and solar power?
choices: They release large amounts of carbon dioxide
They depend on the weather and need storage or backup
check.why: Wind and sunlight release no carbon dioxide while running, but they are not steady, so backup or batteries are needed.

check.q: A phone battery is charged from a wall outlet. Where did that energy come from?
choices: The outlet stores its own energy
The charger created it from nothing
A power plant that changed fuel, wind, sunlight or nuclear energy into electricity
check.why: Energy is conserved. It was stored somewhere first, changed form at the plant, traveled by wire and ended up as chemical energy in the battery.

review.q: A ball's speed triples. By how much does its kinetic energy grow?
review.why: Kinetic energy depends on speed squared, and three times three is nine.

review.q: A coaster train sits at the top of the first hill, barely moving. What kind of energy does it mostly have?
review.why: At the top, the train has lots of height and almost no speed, so its energy is stored as gravitational potential energy.

review.q: Why are the brakes warm at the end of a roller coaster ride?
choices: Friction turned the train's kinetic energy into thermal energy
review.why: Energy is not destroyed. The brakes turned motion into heat, which is where the energy ended up.

review.q: A bathtub of warm water and a cup of boiling water: which statement is true?
choices: The cup has more thermal energy because it is hotter
The tub has more thermal energy, but the cup has the higher temperature
They have the same thermal energy
The tub has the higher temperature
review.why: Temperature is an average per particle. Total thermal energy also depends on how much matter there is, and the tub has far more.

review.q: Which way does heat flow on its own?
choices: From the bigger object to the smaller
review.why: Heat flows from warmer to cooler until the temperatures match. Moving it the other way takes an outside push, like a refrigerator.

review.q: A metal railing and a wooden bench are the same temperature. Why does the metal feel colder?
choices: Metal conducts heat away from your hand faster
Metal is always colder than wood
review.why: Your skin senses how fast it loses heat. Metal conducts quickly, so it feels colder even at the same temperature.

review.q: Which way of heat transfer lets the Sun warm Earth across empty space?
review.why: Radiation travels as light and needs no matter. Conduction and convection both need a material to move through.

review.q: Fat stores about 9 Calories per gram and carbohydrate about 4. What does this tell you?
choices: A gram of fat stores more than twice as much chemical energy as a gram of carbohydrate
review.why: The Calorie is a unit of energy, so more Calories per gram means more stored chemical energy per gram.
